 India's U-23 move: Priorities beyond SAFF
 Published : 2 November 2026
 • 
 Updated : 2 November 2026, 10:40
 • 
 FOOTBALL
 SHARE 
 A
 Anisur Rahman
 Anisur Rahman 
 PHOTO: FACEBOOK 
 To be honest, when India send their U-23 squad, it seems the standard of the championship will fall, but the past record does not suggest so. It is psychological. However, the participation of India's main team changes everything in the SAFF Championship because every participant dreams of clinching the title by beating India.
 Former national footballer and coach Shafiqul Islam Manik 
 The All India Football Federation's (AIFF) decision to send an U-23 developmental squad to the upcoming SAFF Championship raises a pertinent question: are India undermining South Asia's premier football competition, or simply prioritising their long-term ambitions? 
 Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source 
 While other participating nations are expected to field their senior sides, India's approach has sparked debate over the championship's competitiveness. Former national footballer and coach Shafiqul Islam Manik, however, believes the absence of India's senior stars does not necessarily lower the standard.
 "To be honest, when India send their U-23 squad, it seems the standard of the championship will fall, but the past record does not suggest so. It is psychological," Manik said.
 "However, the participation of India's main team changes everything in the SAFF Championship because every participant dreams of clinching the title by beating India."
 History lends weight to part of Manik's argument. India fielded developmental squads in the 2009 and 2018 editions, winning the 2009 title in Dhaka by defeating Maldives before finishing runners-up in 2018 after losing to the same opponents in a penalty shootout.
 India's dominance is undeniable. Of the championship's 14 editions, they have won nine titles, while Maldives have triumphed twice. Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Afghanistan have won once each, leaving Nepal, Pakistan and Bhutan still searching for their maiden crowns.
 Read more India announce second-string squad for SAFF Championship 
 Yet, India's decision cannot be viewed solely through the lens of regional competition. Ranked considerably higher than their South Asian rivals, India have ambitions beyond SAFF. Their primary structural objective is to break into the FIFA top 100 and improve their seeding in Asian Football Confederation (AFC) Asian Cup qualifiers and FIFA World Cup qualifying draws.
 From that perspective, the championship presents a complicated equation. Wins against lower-ranked opponents offer relatively modest FIFA ranking points, while a draw or defeat could prove costly. For a team seeking to establish itself more firmly in Asian football, the risk-reward calculation differs from that facing its regional rivals.
 There are practical considerations, too. Reports suggest India are considering two international friendlies against New Zealand during the November 9-17 FIFA window, which overlaps with the SAFF Championship schedule from November 5-17.
 The timing also creates complications for the Indian Super League (ISL), where clubs may be reluctant to release their first-choice players for a two-week regional tournament. Sending an U-23 squad therefore offers AIFF a compromise: honouring regional commitments without disrupting the domestic calendar or sacrificing opportunities for the senior team to face stronger opposition.
 More importantly, the approach serves India's player-development strategy. The transition from age-group football to senior international competition is difficult, and domestic league performances cannot replicate the pressure of international knockouts, hostile away crowds and regional rivalries.
 India's 2018 campaign demonstrated the potential benefits. Under coach Stephen Constantine, emerging players such as Anirudh Thapa, Lallianzuala Chhangte, Ashique Kuruniyan and Subhasish Bose gained valuable tournament experience, while established figures including Sunil Chhetri, Sandesh Jhingan and Gurpreet Singh Sandhu were left out. Several of those youngsters subsequently became important members of India's senior setup.
 India may therefore have sound reasons for taking this route. But a decision that makes sense for Indian football does not necessarily serve the interests of the SAFF Championship.
 For the region's other contenders, beating India remains a major ambition. Their absence of senior stars may not make the tournament uncompetitive, but it undeniably changes the stakes. India may see SAFF as a platform for developing its next generation; for the rest of the region, it remains a chance to measure themselves against the best.
